title: Sell Mineral Rights in Lowell, OH
metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in Lowell, OH | Washington County
metaDescription: Lowell, Ohio sits on the Muskingum River in Washington County's Utica flank. Learn how riverside farmland and old family tracts get valued for a sale.
heroLead: Lowell sits along the Muskingum River in Washington County, a short drive from Marietta, in territory generally treated as flank acreage relative to the thicker Utica core further east.
intro: Washington County's oil and gas story starts well before the modern shale boom; this is one of the oldest oil-producing regions in the country, with drilling activity going back to the 1860s along the river valleys. Land near Lowell has often been touched by more than one generation of oil and gas leasing, which means the paperwork trail can run deep, and untangling it is usually the real first step before selling.

sections.heading: A long drilling history means layered leases
paragraphs: Because Washington County has been drilled off and on for well over a century, it's not unusual to find multiple historical leases stacked on the same tract near Lowell, some expired, some still technically of record even though no well has produced in decades. A buyer evaluating your interest needs to know which of those old leases, if any, are still legally active before they can put a real number on unleased versus leased minerals.

sections.heading: Where Lowell sits relative to current Utica activity
paragraphs: Modern horizontal Utica/Point Pleasant activity has been heavier in Washington County's northern and eastern reaches than immediately around Lowell itself, so tracts here tend to get valued more conservatively than land closer to Belmont or Monroe County. That doesn't rule out future activity, since operators have continued extending units westward as results from core counties get applied to flank acreage.

sections.heading: Clearing title before you sell
paragraphs: Given the layered leasing history in this area, a title search at the Washington County Recorder's office in Marietta is worth doing early. You want a clear answer on whether any lease is currently active, whether your mineral interest was ever formally severed from the surface, and whether the interest has changed hands through inheritance since the last recorded transaction.

faqs.question: Why does Washington County have so much old lease paperwork?
faqs.answer: It's one of the oldest oil-producing regions in the country, with drilling dating back to the 1860s. Land near Lowell has often been leased more than once over the decades, which can leave old paperwork on record even after leases expire.

faqs.question: Is Lowell in the middle of current Utica drilling?
faqs.answer: Not as heavily as counties to the east like Belmont or Monroe. Lowell is generally treated as flank acreage, though activity has been extending westward over time.

faqs.question: How do I know if an old lease on my land is still active?
faqs.answer: Check whether the lease has a held-by-production clause and whether a well on the unit is still producing. If not, and the primary term has expired, the lease has likely lapsed and your minerals may be open again.
